questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of LSD radix sort?

answer.text: Sort by one digit at a time from least-significant to most-significant, using a stable sort on each digit pass

feedback.text: Correct — LSD processes digits from least to most significant with a stable per-digit sort.

answer.text: Repeatedly swap adjacent elements that are out of order

feedback.text: That is bubble sort.

answer.text: Recursively pick a pivot and partition around it

feedback.text: That is quicksort.

answer.text: Compare full keys with a balanced binary search tree

feedback.text: That is a comparison-based tree sort, not radix sort.

generalfeedback.text: LSD radix sort makes d passes, one per digit from least to most significant, each pass being a stable sort that preserves the order established by earlier passes.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of radix sort, where d = number of digits and k = the base/radix?

feedback.text: Correct — d passes, each a counting sort costing O(n + k).
That is the comparison-sort bound; radix sort is not comparison-based.
Radix sort does not degrade to quadratic time.
That is a single counting-sort pass; radix sort runs d such passes.

generalfeedback.text: Each of the d digit passes is a stable counting sort taking O(n + k), so the total is O(d(n + k)).

questiontext.text: Which stable sort is typically used to sort each digit within LSD radix sort?

feedback.text: Correct — counting sort is stable and linear per digit.
Quicksort is not stable, which would break the per-digit invariant.
Heapsort is not stable and is comparison-based.
Binary search is not a sorting algorithm.

generalfeedback.text: Counting sort is the usual per-digit subroutine because it is stable and runs in O(n + k) per pass.

questiontext.text: LSD radix sort requires that the sort used on each digit be stable for the overall result to be correct.

feedback.text: Correct — stability preserves the ordering from less-significant digits across later passes.
Without a stable per-digit sort, earlier-digit order would be lost.

questiontext.text: Radix sort is a comparison-based algorithm bound by the Ω(n log n) lower bound.

feedback.text: No — it distributes elements by digit values rather than comparing whole keys.

questiontext.text: Which statements about radix sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Its auxiliary space is O(n + k)

feedback.text: Yes — the per-pass counting sort needs an output array of size n and counts of size k.

answer.text: It works well for fixed-width integers or strings

feedback.text: Yes — a bounded number of digits keeps d small.

answer.text: It compares whole keys against one another

feedback.text: No — it distributes by individual digits, not by comparing full keys.

answer.text: An unstable per-digit sort works just as well

feedback.text: No — LSD radix sort requires a stable per-digit sort.

generalfeedback.text: Radix sort uses O(n + k) space, suits fixed-width keys, never compares whole keys, and depends on a stable per-digit sort.
